claim: Septins are conserved cytoskeletal proteins that regulate cell cortex mechanics.
source: Septins are conserved cytoskeletal proteins that regulate cell cortex mechanics.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract summarizing the general function of septins.

claim: Binding to flat lipid membranes requires electrostatic interactions of septins with anionic lipids.
source: binding to flat lipid membranes requires electrostatic interactions of septins with anionic lipids
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing septin binding to PS and PI(4,5)P2-containing membranes.

claim: Membrane binding promotes the ordered self-assembly of fly septins into filamentous meshworks.
source: binding to flat lipid membranes requires electrostatic interactions of septins with anionic lipids and promotes the ordered self-assembly of fly septins into filamentous meshworks
evidence: This is demonstrated through multiple imaging techniques showing filament formation on membranes.

claim: Both fly and mammalian septin hexamers form arrays of single and paired filaments.
source: Transmission electron microscopy reveals that both fly and mammalian septin hexamers form arrays of single and paired filaments.
evidence: This is directly observed in TEM images presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fly filaments form mechanically rigid, 12- to 18-nm thick, double layers of septins.
source: Atomic force microscopy and quartz crystal microbalance demonstrate that the fly filaments form mechanically rigid, 12- to 18-nm thick, double layers of septins.
evidence: This is measured using AFM and QCM-D techniques as described in the results.

claim: C-terminally truncated septin mutants form 4-nm thin monolayers.
source: By contrast, C-terminally truncated septin mutants form 4-nm thin monolayers, indicating that stacking requires the C-terminal coiled coils on DSep2 and Pnut subunits.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with ΔCC mutants showing reduced layer thickness.

claim: Stacking of septin layers requires the C-terminal coiled coils on DSep2 and Pnut subunits.
source: By contrast, C-terminally truncated septin mutants form 4-nm thin monolayers, indicating that stacking requires the C-terminal coiled coils on DSep2 and Pnut subunits.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between full-length and ΔCC mutant septins.

claim: Most of what we currently know about the molecular mechanisms by which septins function comes from studies of the budding yeast cell S. cerevisae.
source: Most of what we currently know about the molecular mechanisms by which septins function comes from studies of the budding yeast cell S. cerevisae, where septins form hetero-octamers (Frazier et al., 1998; Versele et al., 2004; Farkasovsky et al., 2005; Bertin et al., 2008; Khan et al., 2018) that form paired filaments (Byers and Goetsch, 1976; Rodal et al., 2005; Bertin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work on yeast septins.

claim: Yeast septins form hetero-octamers.
source: Most of what we currently know about the molecular mechanisms by which septins function comes from studies of the budding yeast cell S. cerevisae, where septins form hetero-octamers (Frazier et al., 1998; Versele et al., 2004; Farkasovsky et al., 2005; Bertin et al., 2008; Khan et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Yeast septin octamers form paired filaments.
source: where septins form hetero-octamers (Frazier et al., 1998; Versele et al., 2004; Farkasovsky et al., 2005; Bertin et al., 2008; Khan et al., 2018) that form paired filaments (Byers and Goetsch, 1976; Rodal et al., 2005; Bertin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: During budding, septins form a collar encircling the bud neck that acts as a scaffold to recruit proteins necessary for cell division.
source: During budding, septins form a collar encircling the bud neck that acts as a scaffold to recruit proteins necessary for cell division (Longtine et al., 2000; Finnigan et al., 2016; Tamborrini et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on yeast septin function.

claim: Yeast septin collars restrict lateral diffusion of transmembrane proteins.
source: and that restricts lateral diffusion of transmembrane proteins (Barral et al., 2000; Takizawa et al., 2000; Clay et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Animal septins have a much more variable cellular localization than yeast septins that changes with tissue type, developmental stage, and cell cycle state.
source: Compared to yeast septins, animal septins have a much more variable cellular localization that changes with tissue type, developmental stage, and cell cycle state (Bridges and Gladfelter, 2015; Spiliotis, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles on animal septins.

claim: Animal septins are frequently found at curved regions of the plasma membrane such as the base of dendritic spines and cilia.
source: They are frequently found at curved regions of the plasma membrane such as the base of dendritic spines and cilia, where they provide a diffusion barrier (Cho et al., 2011; Ewers et al., 2014; Palander et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Animal septins provide a diffusion barrier at curved membrane regions.
source: They are frequently found at curved regions of the plasma membrane such as the base of dendritic spines and cilia, where they provide a diffusion barrier (Cho et al., 2011; Ewers et al., 2014; Palander et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Animal septins associate with flat regions of the cell cortex where they influence the rigidity and contractility of the actin-myosin cortex within single cells.
source: However, animal septins also associate with flat regions of the cell cortex, where they influence the rigidity and contractility of the actin-myosin cortex within single cells (Tooley et al., 2009; Mostowy et al., 2011; Gilden et al., 2012) and within multicellular tissues (Shindo and Wallingford, 2014; Park et al., 2015; Kim and Cooper, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cortical septins play a key role in cell division where they are needed to stabilize the actomyosin ring.
source: Cortical septins also play a key role in cell division, where they are needed to stabilize the actomyosin ring (Founounou et al., 2013) and recruit proteins that mediate chromosome segregation and abscission (Spiliotis et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2011; Renshaw et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mammalian septins can bind phosphoinositides.
source: Biochemical reconstitution studies have shown that mammalian septins can bind phosphoinositides (Dolat and Spiliotis, 2016; Zhang et al., 1999; Tanaka-Takiguchi et al., 2009; Bridges et al., 2016; Yamada et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous biochemical studies.

claim: Animal septins have been shown to bind actin filaments.
source: but animal septins have also been shown to bind actin filaments (Mavrakis et al., 2014; Dolat et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Animal septins bind various actin-binding proteins including anillin and non-muscle myosin-2.
source: and various actin-binding proteins including anillin (Kinoshita et al., 2002) and non-muscle myosin-2 (Joo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Septin-deficient cells exhibit a markedly reduced cortical rigidity.
source: Septin-deficient cells exhibit a markedly reduced cortical rigidity (Tooley et al., 2009; Mostowy et al., 2011; Gilden et al., 2012; Park et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Septin removal in nondividing cells and tissues leads to dramatic phenotypes consistent with a loss of cortical integrity.
source: Septin removal in nondividing cells and tissues leads to dramatic phenotypes consistent with a loss of cortical integrity, notably the collapse of early gastrulating embryos (Adam et al., 2000), loss of sperm integrity (Kissel et al., 2005; Ihara et al., 2005; Kuo et al., 2015), and defects in neuron morphogenesis (Tada et al., 2007; Xie et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Frog (Xenopus laevis) septins form paired filaments similar to yeast septins.
source: Frog (Xenopus laevis) septins were found to form paired filaments similar to yeast septins (Mendoza et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Recombinant nematode (C. Elegans) septins form bundles.
source: while recombinant nematode (C. Elegans) septins (John et al., 2007) and native and recombinant fly (Drosophila melanogaster) septins (Mavrakis et al., 2014; Field et al., 1996; Huijbregts et al., 2009) were observed to form bundles.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Native and recombinant fly (Drosophila melanogaster) septins form bundles.
source: while recombinant nematode (C. Elegans) septins (John et al., 2007) and native and recombinant fly (Drosophila melanogaster) septins (Mavrakis et al., 2014; Field et al., 1996; Huijbregts et al., 2009) were observed to form bundles.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Recombinant mammalian septin hexamers form rings and spirals that are reminiscent of structures formed by Shs1-capped yeast septin octamers.
source: Recombinant mammalian septin hexamers have been shown to form rings and spirals that are reminiscent of structures formed by Shs1-capped yeast septin octamers (Garcia et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Septin-enriched fractions from porcine brain extracts can tubulate giant liposomes and form filamentous meshworks encasing the membrane tubes.
source: To the best of our knowledge, there are only two reports until now of the organization of animal septins on lipid membranes, showing that septin-enriched fractions from porcine brain extracts can tubulate giant liposomes and form filamentous meshworks encasing the membrane tubes (Tanaka-Takiguchi et al., 2009; Yamada et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PS is the most abundant anionic lipid in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: PS is the most abundant anionic lipid in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (Leventis and Grinstein, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The cell membrane in the fly has been reported to contain 3–10% PS, but the composition varies among tissues and developmental stages.
source: The cell membrane in the fly has been reported to contain 3–10% PS, but the composition varies among tissues and developmental stages (Carvalho et al., 2012; Guan et al., 2013; Jones et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 is an anionic signaling lipid previously shown to interact with yeast and mammalian septins.
source: PI(4,5)P2 is an anionic signaling lipid previously shown to interact with yeast and mammalian septins (Zhang et al., 1999; Bertin et al., 2010; Beber, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 is assumed to be important for septin-membrane interactions in the fly.
source: and assumed to be important for septin-membrane interactions in the fly (Brill et al., 2016; Goldbach et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Fly septin hexamers are highly homologous to their human septin orthologs.
source: which are highly homologous to their human septin orthologs (DSep1, DSep2, and Pnut are 75%, 68%, and 65% identical to SEPT2, SEPT6, and SEPT7, respectively; see Materials and methods section).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis described in the methods.

claim: DSep1 is 75% identical to SEPT2.
source: which are highly homologous to their human septin orthologs (DSep1, DSep2, and Pnut are 75%, 68%, and 65% identical to SEPT2, SEPT6, and SEPT7, respectively; see Materials and methods section).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: DSep2 is 68% identical to SEPT6.
source: which are highly homologous to their human septin orthologs (DSep1, DSep2, and Pnut are 75%, 68%, and 65% identical to SEPT2, SEPT6, and SEPT7, respectively; see Materials and methods section).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Pnut is 65% identical to SEPT7.
source: which are highly homologous to their human septin orthologs (DSep1, DSep2, and Pnut are 75%, 68%, and 65% identical to SEPT2, SEPT6, and SEPT7, respectively; see Materials and methods section).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Fly septin hexamers have a palindromic arrangement with the Pnut subunits in the center, the DSep1 subunits at the termini, and the DSep2 subunits in between.
source: Based on phylogenetic analysis that classifies fly and human septins in distinct subgroups (DSep1/SEPT2 in the SEPT2 subgroup; DSep2/SEPT6 in the SEPT6 subgroup; Pnut/SEPT7 in the SEPT7 subgroup Cao et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2007), and the recently demonstrated order of subunits in mammalian septin complexes (Mendonça et al., 2019; Soroor et al., 2021; DeRose et al., 2020), fly septin hexamers should have a palindromic arrangement with the Pnut subunits in the center, the DSep1 subunits at the termini, and the DSep2 subunits in between (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analysis and previous studies on mammalian septins.

claim: The C-terminus of DSep1 is predicted to form a coiled-coil that is 28 residues long.
source: Using the coiled-coil prediction algorithm COILS (see Materials and methods section), we predict the C-terminus of DSep1 to form a coiled-coil that is 28 residues long
evidence: This is based on computational prediction using the COILS algorithm.

claim: The C-termini of Pnut and DSep2 are predicted to form coiled-coils that are 86 residues long.
source: and the C-termini of Pnut and DSep2 to form coiled-coils that are 86 residues long (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction using the COILS algorithm.

claim: The coiled-coil of DSep1/SEPT2 is estimated to be 4 nm long.
source: Considering a 1.5 Å rise per residue in an alpha-helix, we estimate the coiled-coil of DSep1/SEPT2 to be 4 nm long
evidence: This is calculated based on the predicted coiled-coil length and structural parameters.

claim: The coiled-coils of DSep2/SEPT6 and Pnut/SEPT7 are estimated to be 13 nm long.
source: and the coiled-coils of DSep2/SEPT6 and Pnut/SEPT7 to be 13 nm long (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is calculated based on the predicted coiled-coil length and structural parameters.

claim: Hexamers form 24-nm-long rods, with the globular domains (G-domains) of the septin subunits approximately 4 nm in diameter.
source: Hexamers form 24-nm-long rods, with the globular domains (G-domains) of the septin subunits approximately 4 nm in diameter (Mavrakis et al., 2014; Sirajuddin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Septin hexamers did not form any structures visible at the resolution of the light microscope until the concentration reached 200 nM.
source: As shown in Figure 1D, septin hexamers did not form any structures visible at the resolution of the light microscope until the concentration reached 200 nM.
evidence: This is directly observed in TIRF imaging experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: When septin concentration was increased to 500 nM, the septin hexamers formed longer bundles.
source: When we increased the concentration further to 500 nM, the septin hexamers formed longer bundles.
evidence: This is observed in TIRF imaging experiments.

claim: Bundle formation was very rapid, taking less than 2 min for completion.
source: Bundle formation was very rapid, taking less than 2 min for completion.
evidence: This is observed in TIRF imaging experiments.

claim: The septin bundles were rather straight and did not exhibit measurable thermal bending undulations, indicating that they must be stiff.
source: The bundles were rather straight and did not exhibit measurable thermal bending undulations, indicating that they must be stiff.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of bundle morphology in TIRF images.

claim: Yeast septins form thin semiflexible polymers with an average mass-per-length of ~20 kDa/nm.
source: As shown in Figure 1E, the yeast septins form thin semiflexible polymers that are weaker in intensity than the TMV rods, consistent with their smaller mass per length (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B). The average mass-per-length (based on 10 septin filaments from three images) was ~20 kDa/nm, close to the mass-per-length expected for paired filaments.
evidence: This is measured using STEM imaging with TMV rods as mass standards.

claim: Yeast septin filaments occasionally show a double-stranded structure with two filaments running in parallel with a spacing in the range of 17–27 nm.
source: In rare cases, the image clearly showed a double-stranded structure with two filaments running in parallel with a small spacing in the range of 17–27 nm, consistent with prior transmission EM findings (Bertin et al., 2008) (see lower panel of Figure 1E).
evidence: This is observed in STEM images and consistent with previous EM studies.

claim: Fly septin bundles formed at 200 nM had tapered ends and a thicker center.
source: Bundles formed at 200 nM had tapered ends and a thicker center.
evidence: This is observed in STEM images.

claim: A fly septin bundle formed at 200 nM has a MPL of around 250 kDa/nm in the center and a corresponding center width of 31 nm.
source: The example bundle in Figure 1F has a MPL of around 250 kDa/nm in the center (marked by an asterisk) and a corresponding center width of 31 nm.
evidence: This is measured from STEM images.

claim: A fly septin bundle with MPL of 250 kDa/nm and width of 31 nm translates to around 20 hexamers per cross-section.
source: Given a calculated MPL of 12.8 kDa/nm per fly septin hexamer, this number translates to around 20 hexamers per cross-section.
evidence: This is calculated from the measured MPL and known hexamer mass.

claim: A width of 31 nm and 20 hexamers per cross-section implies there are at least three monolayers of septins.
source: Considering that the inter-filament spacing has to be at least 4 nm, a width of 31 nm and 20 hexamers per cross-section implies there are at least three monolayers.
evidence: This is inferred from geometric considerations.

claim: At 500 nM, fly septin bundles had maximal widths of up to 280 nm and MPL values up to ~5000 kDa/nm.
source: At 500 nM, the septin bundles were thicker (Figure 1G) with maximal widths of up to 280 nm and MPL values up to ~5000 kDa/nm (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), corresponding to >400 hexamers per cross-section or a thickness of at least six monolayers.
evidence: This is measured from STEM images.

claim: Septin bundles in solution do not grow as flat sheets but as 3D bundles.
source: This analysis suggests that septin bundles in solution do not grow as flat sheets but as 3D bundles.
evidence: This is inferred from the STEM analysis of bundle dimensions.

claim: Already at 1% PI(4,5)P2, septin hexamers formed immobile bundles adhering to the membrane.
source: Already at 1% PI(4,5)P2, septin hexamers formed immobile bundles adhering to the membrane (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is observed in TIRF imaging experiments.

claim: Membrane recruitment of septins was observed in the absence of methylcellulose, showing that septin hexamers indeed bind to PI(4,5)P2 lipids.
source: Importantly, membrane recruitment was observed here in the absence of methylcellulose, showing that septin hexamers indeed bind to PI(4,5)P2 lipids.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF imaging without methylcellulose.

claim: As the PI(4,5)P2 content was raised from 1% to 8%, there was a striking transition from a sparse arrangement of thick bundles to a dense protein layer.
source: As we raised the PI(4,5)P2 content from 1% to 8%, we observed a striking transition from a sparse arrangement of thick bundles to a dense protein layer.
evidence: This is observed in TIRF imaging experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Fly septin hexamers were also recruited to PS-containing bilayers and showed a transition from a sparse distribution of thick bundles at low PS content to a dense layer at high PS content.
source: As shown in Figure 2C, fly septin hexamers were also recruited to the PS-containing bilayers and again showed a transition from a sparse distribution of thick bundles at low PS content to a dense layer at high PS content.
evidence: This is observed in TIRF imaging experiments.

claim: The filamentous septin structures were already present as soon as imaging could start (~3 min after septin loading) and did not change in number or thickness over time.
source: The filamentous septin structures were already present as soon as we could start imaging (~3 min after septin loading into the flow channel) and the structures did not change in number or thickness over time (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed in time-lapse TIRF imaging.

claim: The total fluorescence intensity of membrane-bound septins linearly increased as the PS content was raised from 5% to 20%.
source: The total fluorescence intensity, which is a proxy for the amount of membrane-bound septins, linearly increased as the PS content was raised from 5% to 20% (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is measured from TIRF imaging experiments.

claim: The observation that PS has a qualitatively similar effect compared to PI(4,5)P2 on septin recruitment and assembly suggests that the membrane-binding affinity of fly septin hexamers is governed by the net surface charge of the membrane rather than by any specific affinity for PI(4,5)P2.
source: The observation that PS has a qualitatively similar effect compared to PI(4,5)P2 on septin recruitment and assembly on SLBs suggests that the membrane-binding affinity of fly septin hexamers is governed by the net surface charge of the membrane rather than by any specific affinity for PI(4,5)P2.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of septin behavior on PS vs PI(4,5)P2 membranes.

claim: The transition from dilute septin bundles to dense septin films required a larger PS mole fraction (10%) than PI(4,5)P2 (2.5%).
source: The transition from dilute septin bundles to dense septin films required a larger PS mole fraction (10%) than PI(4,5)P2 (2.5%), consistent with the larger net charge (−4) of the head group of PI(4,5)P2 due to the phosphate groups compared to the net charge (−1) on the head group of PS (Blin et al., 2008; Kooijman et al., 2009; Toner et al., 1988; Graber et al., 2012).
evidence: This is observed in TIRF experiments and consistent with known lipid charges.

claim: At low septin concentrations (10–50 nM), dim puncta and brighter puncta indicative of protein aggregation were observed.
source: At low concentrations (10–50 nM), we observed dim puncta and also brighter puncta, indicative of protein aggregation (note that images are contrast-inverted).
evidence: This is observed in TIRF imaging experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: When septin concentration was increased to values of 100 nM and higher, a fibrillar meshwork of septin filaments was suddenly observed.
source: Remarkably, when we increased the septin concentration to values of 100 nM and higher, we suddenly observed a fibrillar meshwork of septin filaments.
evidence: This is observed in TIRF imaging experiments.

claim: At concentrations above 200 nM, septin bundles were present in the solution above the bilayer in addition to the membrane-bound septin meshwork.
source: At concentrations above 200 nM, we found by off-TIRF-angle imaging that, in addition to the membrane-bound septin meshwork, also septin bundles were present in the solution above the bilayer, consistent with the observed onset for bundling in the absence of an adhesive membrane (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is observed by off-TIRF-angle imaging.

claim: Membrane-bound septins exhibited negligible subunit exchange.
source: Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching experiments showed that the membrane-bound septins exhibited negligible subunit exchange (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), indicating that they are stably anchored to the membrane.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments.

claim: The membrane underneath the septin film was fluid, as indicated by FRAP measurements of rhodamine-labeled PE tracer lipids.
source: The membrane underneath the septin film was nevertheless fluid, as indicated by FRAP measurements of rhodamine-labeled PE tracer lipids (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments on lipids.

claim: Septin hexamers formed densely packed arrays of thin filaments on lipid monolayers containing PS, PI(4,5)P2, or both.
source: As shown in Figure 3A–C, septin hexamers formed densely packed arrays of thin filaments in all three cases, which is qualitatively consistent with the dense meshworks observed by TIRF microscopy.
evidence: This is observed in TEM images.

claim: Close inspection of the EM micrographs revealed paired septin filaments with an average center-to-center spacing of 5.7 ± 0.8 nm on monolayers containing PS plus PI(4,5)P2.
source: Close inspection of the EM micrographs revealed paired septin filaments (black arrows point out examples) with an average center-to-center spacing of 5.7 ± 0.8 nm on monolayers containing PS plus PIP(4,5)P2 (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is measured from TEM images.

claim: The width of individual septin filaments was in the range of 3.5–4 nm (3.6 ± 0.53 nm averaged over all lipid conditions).
source: The width of the individual filaments was in the range of 3.5–4 nm (3.6 ± 0.53 nm (N = 60) averaged over all lipid conditions; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), consistent with the expected 4 nm width of fly septin hexamers (Mavrakis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is measured from TEM images and consistent with previous structural data.

claim: On monolayers containing 20% PS plus 5% PI(4,5)P2, paired filaments were bridged at intervals of 24 nm by single or double hexamer rods.
source: On monolayers containing 20% PS plus 5% PI(4,5)P2, we could observe clear examples of paired filaments that were bridged at intervals of 24 nm by single or double hexamer rods (Figure 3C), recognizable by their lengths clustering around either 24 nm or 48 nm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), respectively.
evidence: This is observed in TEM images.

claim: Bridges between paired filaments were either perpendicular to the filaments they bridged or under an angle.
source: These bridges were either perpendicular to the filaments they bridged (blue arrowheads) or under an angle (red arrowheads; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1C for quantification).
evidence: This is observed in TEM images.

claim: Mammalian septin hexamers form comparable arrays of tightly paired filaments connected by orthogonally or diagonally oriented single filaments on lipid monolayers.
source: We observed comparable arrays of tightly paired filaments connected by orthogonally or diagonally oriented single filaments for mammalian septins on lipid monolayers of the same composition (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in TEM images of mammalian septins.

claim: Similar arrays of filaments were previously observed for budding yeast septins.
source: Similar arrays of filaments were previously also observed for budding yeast septins (Garcia et al., 2011; Bertin et al., 2010), suggesting that this architectural feature is conserved within eukaryotes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on yeast septins.

claim: For mammalian septin hexamers, the paired filaments are intersected with a distinct set of thinner continuous filaments, creating a network of interconnected and perpendicular filaments.
source: Instead, for the mammalian septin hexamers, the paired filaments (white arrows in Figure 3—figure supplement 2) are intersected with a distinct set of thinner continuous filaments (red arrows), creating a network of interconnected and perpendicular filaments.
evidence: This is observed in TEM images of mammalian septins.

claim: CryoEM images confirm the presence of paired septin filaments on PI(4,5)P2-containing lipid membranes.
source: As shown in Figure 4, the cryoEM images confirm the presence of paired septin filaments on PI(4,5)P2-containing lipid membranes (examples are traced out by double red lines in Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is observed in cryoEM images.

claim: The average center-to-center distance between filaments forming a pair in cryoEM was 5.7 ± 0.8 nm.
source: The average center-to-center distance between the filaments forming a pair was 5.7 ± 0.8 nm (N = 40, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), in excellent agreement with the negative stain images of septin filaments on lipid monolayers.
evidence: This is measured from cryoEM images.

claim: Single filaments or hexamers were occasionally observed in cryoEM, including some that appeared to interconnect filaments at an orthogonal or oblique angle.
source: In addition, we occasionally observed single filaments or hexamers (examples are traced out by single red lines in Figure 4B) including some that appeared to interconnect filaments at an orthogonal or oblique angle (blue lines in Figure 4B).
evidence: This is observed in cryoEM images.

claim: The diameter of control vesicles was measured to be 358 ± 180 nm while the diameter of vesicles displaying septins was 542 ± 199 nm.
source: An indication for curvature-dependent binding in our data is that the diameter of control vesicles was measured to be 358 ± 180 nm (N = 40) while the diameter of similar vesicles displaying septins was 542 ± 199 nm (N = 24), thus slightly higher, on average (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is measured from cryoEM images.

claim: Vesicles decorated with septin filaments typically appeared to have a faceted contour, whereas vesicles alone usually retained their spherical shape in cryoEM.
source: Vesicles decorated with septin filaments typically appeared to have a faceted contour, whereas vesicles alone usually retained their spherical shape in cryoEM.
evidence: This is observed in cryoEM images.

claim: Cryo-electron tomography gave clear evidence that septin filaments are membrane-bound.
source: Cryo-electron tomography gave further clear evidence that septin filaments are indeed membrane-bound (see Figure 4C–D and Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cryo-tomography.

claim: At 12 nM, septin hexamers formed threads of typically several micrometers in length that were sparsely and randomly distributed on the bilayer surface.
source: At 12 nM, septin hexamers formed threads of typically several micrometers in length that were sparsely and randomly distributed on the bilayer surface (Figure 5A–B, left column).
evidence: This is observed in AFM images.

claim: At 12 nM, the apparent height of septin threads was mostly uniform at 5.1 ± 0.9 nm with a few notable exceptions around 12 nm.
source: Their apparent height was mostly uniform at 5.1 ± 0.9 nm (N = 29), with a few notable exceptions around 12 nm (N = 2).
evidence: This is measured from AFM images.

claim: At 12 nM, most isolated threads had a width of 11.5 ± 1.6 nm while merged threads were wider (16.6 ± 0.9 nm).
source: The apparent width showed two relatively broad but distinct populations: most isolated threads had a width of 11.5 ± 1.6 nm (N = 19), whereas all merged threads and a few isolated ones were wider (16.6 ± 0.9 nm; N = 12) (Figure 5C, left column, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is measured from AFM images.

claim: At 24 nM, septin hexamers formed threads that were isolated in some places and concentrated in areas of enhanced density in other places.
source: At 24 nM, septin hexamers formed threads that were isolated in some places and concentrated in areas of enhanced density in other places (Figure 5A–B, center column).
evidence: This is observed in AFM images.

claim: At 60 nM, the septin hexamers formed threads that densely covered the bilayer surface in closely apposed patches of aligned filaments, resembling nematic domains.
source: At 60 nM, the septin hexamers formed threads that densely covered the bilayer surface (Figure 5A–B, right column) in closely apposed patches of aligned filaments, resembling nematic domains observed for other 2D arrays of densely packed semiflexible biopolymers (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is observed in AFM images.

claim: At 60 nM, the smallest thread heights and widths observed were comparable to those observed at 12 nM, indicating isolated single or paired filaments were still present.
source: The smallest thread heights and widths observed were comparable to those observed at 12 nM, indicating isolated single or paired filaments were still present.
evidence: This is measured from AFM images.

claim: At 60 nM, some threads appeared much wider (up to a few 100 nm) suggesting that many single filaments may closely align on the lipid membrane.
source: Other threads appeared much wider (up to a few 100 nm; Figure 5C, right column). This suggests that many (up to several tens of) single filaments may closely align on the lipid membrane, although the lateral resolution was insufficient to reveal the individual filaments and their spacing.
evidence: This is measured from AFM images.

claim: At 60 nM, wider threads had an elevated height, mostly between 8 and 13 nm and occasionally up to 18 nm, suggesting that septins also stacked on top of each other.
source: The wider threads also had an elevated height, mostly between 8 and 13 nm and occasionally up to 18 nm (Figure 5C, right column), suggesting that septins also stacked on top of each other.
evidence: This is measured from AFM images.

claim: The morphologies of unfixed septins resembled those of GTA-fixed ones, though imaging unfixed septins was challenging because the filaments were more easily disrupted by the AFM tip.
source: Importantly, the morphologies of unfixed septins resembled those of GTA-fixed ones, though imaging in this case was challenging because the filaments were more easily disrupted by the AFM tip (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed by comparing AFM images of fixed and unfixed samples.

claim: Isolated filaments had heights of 4 nm, corresponding to the height of a single septin hexamer and thus a single layer of septin filaments.
source: Here, we observed that the isolated filaments had heights of 4 nm, corresponding to the height of a single septin hexamer and thus a single layer of septin filaments, while the bundled areas had heights between 8 nm and 12 nm, suggesting that septin filaments can stack on top of each other.
evidence: This is measured from AFM images.

claim: Bundled areas had heights between 8 nm and 12 nm, suggesting that septin filaments can stack on top of each other.
source: while the bundled areas had heights between 8 nm and 12 nm, suggesting that septin filaments can stack on top of each other.
evidence: This is measured from AFM images.

claim: In sparsely covered bilayer regions, wider bundles generally remained stable whereas narrower bundles or isolated filaments sometimes appeared ragged, suggesting that the AFM tip moved them along the membrane.
source: In sparsely covered bilayer regions, wider bundles generally remained stable whereas narrower bundles or isolated filaments (both GTA-fixed and unfixed) sometimes appeared ragged, suggesting that the AFM tip moved them along the membrane (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is observed in consecutive AFM scans.

claim: Densely covered regions formed at 60 nM septins were completely unchanged after three consecutive 10 min scans, both for GTA-fixed and unfixed samples.
source: Densely covered regions formed at 60 nM septins were completely unchanged after three consecutive 10 min scans, again both for GTA-fixed and unfixed samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is observed in consecutive AFM scans.

claim: Lateral associations among septin filaments within bundles or dense arrays may cause mechanical stabilization.
source: These observations suggest that lateral associations among septin filaments within bundles or dense arrays may cause mechanical stabilization.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that dense arrays are more stable than isolated filaments.

claim: Entire bundles can be laterally displaced along the membrane owing to lateral forces exerted by the AFM tip, resulting in permanent local kinks.
source: Some image sequences clearly showed that entire bundles can be laterally displaced along the membrane owing to lateral forces exerted by the AFM tip. Interestingly, these events did not destroy the bundles but resulted in permanent local kinks, suggesting the septin filaments are intrinsically stiff and ductile but the link to the membrane is fluid.
evidence: This is observed in consecutive AFM scans shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Septin filaments are intrinsically stiff and ductile but the link to the membrane is fluid.
source: Interestingly, these events did not destroy the bundles but resulted in permanent local kinks, suggesting the septin filaments are intrinsically stiff and ductile but the link to the membrane is fluid.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of bundle displacement without destruction.

claim: The maximum thickness of the septin films at 60 nM was approximately 18 nm according to AFM height profiles.
source: The maximum thickness of the septin films at 60 nM was approximately 18 nm, according to the height profiles.
evidence: This is measured from AFM images.

claim: SUV perfusion on a plain silica surface caused immediate changes in Δf and ΔD in a two-stage process characteristic for the initial adsorption of intact SUVs followed by SUV rupture, spreading and coalescence.
source: SUV perfusion on a plain silica surface (Figure 7A) caused immediate changes in Δf and ΔD in a two-stage process that is characteristic for the initial adsorption of intact SUVs to the sensor surface followed by SUV rupture, spreading and coalescence (Richter et al., 2006).
evidence: This is observed in QCM-D measurements and consistent with known SLB formation mechanisms.

claim: The final shifts of Δf = −25 ± 1 Hz and ΔD < 0.2 × 10−6 are typical for confluent SLBs composed of PC and PS of high quality.
source: The final shifts of Δf = −25 ± 1 Hz and ΔD < 0.2 × 10−6 (N = 6) are typical for confluent SLBs composed of PC and PS of high quality, that is, with a negligible quantity of residual intact vesicles (Richter et al., 2003).
evidence: This is measured by QCM-D and consistent with previous characterization of SLBs.

claim: Septin hexamer perfusion at 60 nM on SLBs produced an immediate decrease of Δf and a concurrent increase of ΔD, indicating that septins adsorbed.
source: Septin hexamer perfusion at 60 nM on such a SLB (Figure 7B) produced an immediate decrease of Δf and a concurrent increase of ΔD, indicating that septins adsorbed.
evidence: This is observed in QCM-D measurements.

claim: Septin binding reached a plateau after about 50 min, and subsequent perfusion with buffer caused no appreciable change in Δf, suggesting that septin hexamers stably adsorb to the membrane.
source: Binding reached a plateau after about 50 min, and subsequent perfusion with buffer caused no appreciable change in Δf, suggesting that septin hexamers stably adsorb to the membrane.
evidence: This is observed in QCM-D measurements.

claim: The saturation of the QCM-D signal despite continued perfusion with septin hexamers indicates the presence of a mechanism that limits septin binding and film growth.
source: Moreover, the saturation of the signal despite continued perfusion with septin hexamers indicates the presence of a mechanism that limits septin binding and film growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the QCM-D data showing signal saturation.

claim: Similar binding kinetics and self-limiting levels of binding were observed on SLBs containing 5% PI(4,5)P2, or a combination of 5% PI(4,5)P2 and 20% PS.
source: We observed similar binding kinetics and self-limiting levels of binding on SLBs containing 5% PI(4,5)P2, or a combination of 5% PI(4,5)P2 and 20% PS (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is observed in QCM-D measurements.

claim: No adhesion of septin hexamers to pure PC membranes was observed.
source: In contrast, we did not observe any adhesion of septin hexamers to pure PC membranes (Figure 7B; dotted blue line with diamonds).
evidence: This is observed in QCM-D measurements.

claim: The presence of negatively charged lipids is required for septin-membrane binding.
source: We conclude that the presence of negatively charged lipids is required for septin-membrane binding, consistent with the TIRF observations, and that film growth is self-limiting.
evidence: This is concluded from QCM-D and TIRF experiments.

claim: The total frequency shift for septin binding was Δf = -93 ± 4 Hz on SLBs containing 20%PS.
source: The total frequency shift for septin binding was Δf = -93 ± 4 Hz (N = 4) on SLBs containing 20%PS
evidence: This is measured by QCM-D.

claim: The total frequency shift for septin binding was Δf = -77 ± 2 Hz on SLBs containing 5% PI(4,5)P2.
source: Δf = -77 ± 2 Hz (N = 2) on SLBs containing 5% PI(4,5)P2
evidence: This is measured by QCM-D.

claim: The total frequency shift for septin binding was Δf = -113 ± 7 Hz on SLBs containing both 5% PI(4,5)P2 and 20% PS.
source: and Δf = -113 ± 7 Hz (N = 2) on SLBs containing both 5% PI(4,5)P2 and 20% PS (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is measured by QCM-D.

claim: Using the Sauerbrey equation, septin film thickness values are estimated to be 15 nm on SLBs containing 20% PS, 13 nm on SLBs containing 5% PI(4,5)P2, and 19 nm on SLBs containing both 5% PI(4,5)P2 and 20% PS.
source: Using the Sauerbrey equation (see Eq. (1) Nishihama et al., 2011), we estimate septin film thickness values of 15 nm on SLBs containing 20% PS, 13 nm on SLBs containing 5% PI(4,5)P2, and 19 nm on SLBs containing both 5% PI(4,5)P2 and 20% PS, from the respective frequency shifts.
evidence: This is calculated from QCM-D frequency shifts using the Sauerbrey equation.

claim: The estimated film thicknesses from QCM-D are consistent with the upper end of bundle heights measured by AFM.
source: This is consistent with the upper end of bundle heights measured by AFM (Figure 5C, right column), which we had attributed to stacking into more than one layer.
evidence: This is a comparison between QCM-D and AFM measurements.

claim: Membrane-bound septins attained dissipation over frequency shift ratios ΔD/-Δf between (0.20 ± 0.01)×10−6/Hz at low coverage and (0.09 ± 0.01)×10−6/Hz at high coverage.
source: Membrane-bound septins attained dissipation over frequency shift ratios ΔD/-Δf between (0.20 ± 0.01)×10−6/Hz at low coverage (Δf = −15 ± 5 Hz) and (0.09 ± 0.01)×10−6/Hz at high coverage (Δf < −90 Hz; N = 4; Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is measured from QCM-D data.

claim: The higher ΔD/-Δf ratios for septins are consistent with a high degree of flexibility in the linkage between the coiled coils and the globular domains of septin hexamers.
source: The higher ΔD/-Δf ratios for septins are consistent with a high degree of flexibility in the linkage between the coiled coils and the globular domains of septin hexamers.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of ΔD/-Δf ratios with other proteins.

claim: C-terminally truncated fly septin hexamers (ΔCC mutant) form stable hexamers.
source: Transmission EM confirmed that fly septins with their C-termini truncated from all subunits form stable hexamers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), similarly to C-terminally truncated human septin hexamers (Sirajuddin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is observed in TEM images and consistent with previous studies on human septins.

claim: In low salt polymerization buffer, the ΔCC mutant only formed short rods with lengths varying continuously between ~20 and ~80 nm.
source: EM imaging showed that in low salt polymerization buffer, the ΔCC mutant only formed short rods (Figure 8A–B) with lengths varying continuously between ~20 and ~80 nm (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in TEM images.

claim: On lipid monolayers, the C-terminally truncated fly septin hexamers formed dense arrays of aligned filaments.
source: However, on lipid monolayers the C-terminally truncated fly septin hexamers formed dense arrays of aligned filaments (Figure 8C–F).
evidence: This is observed in TEM images.

claim: Membrane-binding promotes filament formation for C-terminally truncated septins, mirroring earlier observations for yeast septin octamers with C-terminally truncated Cdc11 subunits.
source: Thus, membrane-binding promotes filament formation, mirroring earlier observations for yeast septin octamers with C-terminally truncated Cdc11 subunits (Bertin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with yeast septin behavior.

claim: The width of the ΔCC septin filaments was on average slightly smaller than that of full length septin filaments, around 3.5 nm.
source: The width of the ΔCC septin filaments was on average slightly smaller than that of full length septin filaments, around 3.5 nm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), likely due to the absence of coiled coils.
evidence: This is measured from TEM images.

claim: In some places, three ΔCC septin filaments can be seen side by side instead of two.
source: In places we can see three filaments side by side instead of two (indicated by triple blue lines in Figure 8D).
evidence: This is observed in TEM images.

claim: The mutant ΔCC filaments were more closely spaced than wild type septin filaments, with a center-to-center distance for filaments within pairs of around 4.5 nm.
source: The mutant filaments were even more closely spaced than wild type septin filaments, with a center-to-center distance for filaments within pairs of around 4.5 nm (Figure 8G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), consistent with direct contact between the globular domains deprived of the CC domain of adjacent filaments due to crowding and perhaps specific G-domain interactions.
evidence: This is measured from TEM images.

claim: The septin density on the lipid monolayers observed in EM images for the ΔCC mutant was notably higher than for the full-length septins, even though the solution concentrations were the same.
source: The septin density on the lipid monolayers observed in EM images for the ΔCC mutant was notably higher than for the full-length septins, even though the solution concentrations were the same.
evidence: This is observed by comparing TEM images of ΔCC and full-length septins.

claim: The ΔCC mutant binds to bilayers but the frequency shift is much smaller than for the full-length septins, indicating a thinner layer.
source: As shown in Figure 7C, the ΔCC mutant binds to the bilayers but the frequency shift is much smaller than for the full-length septins, indicating a thinner layer.
evidence: This is measured by QCM-D.

claim: For the ΔCC mutant, the -Δf values remained less than 10 Hz, consistent with a single septin monolayer.
source: In this case, the -Δf values remained less than 10 Hz, consistent with a single septin monolayer.
evidence: This is measured by QCM-D.

claim: The coiled coils are not needed for membrane binding, but they are needed for filament pairing, the formation of cross-bridges, and the stacking of septins on top of each other.
source: Thus, the EM and QCM-D data demonstrate that the coiled coils are not needed for membrane binding, but they are needed for filament pairing, the formation of cross-bridges, and the stacking of septins on top of each other.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of ΔCC and full-length septin behavior.

claim: Fly septin hexamers have a high affinity for negatively charged lipid bilayers, which competes with the septin–septin lateral interactions that prevail in bulk solution.
source: Fluorescence imaging revealed that fly septin hexamers have a high affinity for negatively charged lipid bilayers, which competes with the septin–septin lateral interactions that prevail in bulk solution, and that they form dense membrane-associated meshworks.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF imaging experiments.

claim: Fly septin hexamers form dense membrane-associated meshworks.
source: Fluorescence imaging revealed that fly septin hexamers have a high affinity for negatively charged lipid bilayers, which competes with the septin–septin lateral interactions that prevail in bulk solution, and that they form dense membrane-associated meshworks.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF imaging experiments.

claim: Electron microscopy imaging revealed that septin meshworks are predominantly comprised of paired filaments and meshworks thereof.
source: Electron microscopy (EM) imaging revealed that these meshworks are predominantly comprised of paired filaments and meshworks thereof.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TEM and cryoEM imaging.

claim: A similar organization of paired filaments was observed for mammalian septin hexamers.
source: A similar organization was observed for mammalian septin hexamers, consistent with earlier findings for septin-containing porcine brain extracts (Tanaka-Takiguchi et al., 2009; Yamada et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TEM imaging and consistent with previous studies.

claim: Atomic force microscopy of septins on lipid bilayers showed that septin filaments laterally associate into bundles but also stack on top of each other.
source: Finally, atomic force microscopy (AFM) of septins on lipid bilayers showed that septin filaments laterally associate into bundles but also stack on top of each other.
evidence: This is demonstrated by AFM imaging.

claim: AFM imaging, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching and QCM-D experiments indicate that the septins are immobile and firmly attached to the membrane.
source: AFM imaging, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching and QCM-D experiments indicate that the septins are immobile and firmly attached to the membrane.
evidence: This is demonstrated by multiple experimental techniques.

claim: C-terminally truncated septin hexamers form monolayers and the filaments do not form pairs and meshworks, showing that the coiled coils of septins are crucial for mediating septin-septin interactions.
source: By contrast, C-terminally truncated septin hexamers form monolayers and the filaments do not form pairs and meshworks, showing that the coiled coils of septins are crucial for mediating septin-septin interactions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with ΔCC mutants.

claim: Membrane binding catalyzes animal septin polymerization.
source: Our findings establish that membrane binding catalyzes animal septin polymerization and has a dramatic impact on septin self-assembly, with C-terminal coiled-coils playing a key role in higher order septin filament organization.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of septin assembly in solution vs on membranes.

claim: Membrane binding has a dramatic impact on septin self-assembly.
source: Our findings establish that membrane binding catalyzes animal septin polymerization and has a dramatic impact on septin self-assembly, with C-terminal coiled-coils playing a key role in higher order septin filament organization.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental observations.

claim: C-terminal coiled-coils play a key role in higher order septin filament organization.
source: Our findings establish that membrane binding catalyzes animal septin polymerization and has a dramatic impact on septin self-assembly, with C-terminal coiled-coils playing a key role in higher order septin filament organization.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of full-length and ΔCC mutant septins.

claim: For fly septin hexamers, the threshold for polymerization is lowered more than 10-fold, from 200 nM in solution to less than 12 nM on negatively charged membranes.
source: For fly septin hexamers, the threshold for polymerization is lowered more than 10-fold, from 200 nM in solution to less than 12 nM on negatively charged membranes (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing TIRF and AFM data for septins in solution vs on membranes.

claim: The polymerization-enhancing effect of membrane binding is likely due to the increase of the effective septin concentration caused by 2D confinement.
source: The polymerization-enhancing effect of membrane binding is likely due to the increase of the effective septin concentration caused by 2D confinement.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on general principles of 2D confinement.

claim: Membrane binding may orient septins in a manner that promotes their polymerization, as seen for other proteins such as annexin A5.
source: In addition, membrane binding may orient septins in a manner that promotes their polymerization, as seen for other proteins such as annexin A5 (Oling et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by analogy to other proteins.

claim: Both animal and yeast septins form paired filaments visible by transmission electron microscopy, with a narrow spacing of ~2 nm.
source: A second similarity between the behavior of animal and yeast septins on membranes is that they both form paired filaments visible by transmission electron microscopy, with a narrow spacing of ~2 nm, much narrower than the ~10 nm spacing observed for yeast septin filaments formed in solution (Bertin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is observed in TEM images and compared to previous studies on yeast septins.

claim: Paired filaments of both animal and yeast septins are interconnected by bridges visible by electron microscopy, which appear to be formed by short and thin (single) septin filaments having a length and axial spacing that correspond to the length of a single protomer.
source: A third similarity is that paired filaments of both animal and yeast septins are interconnected by bridges visible by electron microscopy, which appear to be formed by short and thin (single) septin filaments having a length and axial spacing that correspond to the length of a single protomer (Bertin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is observed in TEM images and compared to previous studies on yeast septins.

claim: Similar arrays of septin filaments have been observed by electron microscopy in yeast cells.
source: Similar arrays have been observed by electron microscopy in yeast cells (Ong et al., 2014), but not yet in animal cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Fly septins form thick and rigid bundles with tapered ends in solution, suggesting that the septins have strong lateral interactions that promote bundling.
source: Fly septins form thick and rigid bundles with tapered ends in solution, suggesting that the septins have strong lateral interactions that promote bundling.
evidence: This is observed in TIRF and STEM imaging.

claim: On membranes, there is a gradual transition from dilute arrays of thick bundles to dense arrays of paired filaments with increasing net surface charge, suggesting a competition of septin-membrane interactions with lateral septin-septin interactions.
source: On membranes, however, we observed by TIRF microscopy a gradual transition from dilute arrays of thick bundles to dense arrays of paired filaments with increasing net surface charge. This observation suggests a competition of septin-membrane interactions with lateral septin-septin interactions, which suppresses the formation of thick bundles on membranes.
evidence: This is observed in TIRF imaging experiments.

claim: Yeast septin octamers tend to form paired filaments in solution.
source: By contrast, yeast septin octamers tend to form paired filaments in solution (Bertin et al., 2008; Bertin et al., 2010) (as confirmed by quantitative mass-mapping STEM in our study, see Figure 1E), although they do form bundles under certain conditions (Booth and Thorner, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by STEM in this study.

claim: In solution fly septins have a stronger propensity for bundling than yeast septins, but on membranes the two septins behave similarly.
source: Thus, in solution fly septins have a stronger propensity for bundling than yeast septins, but on membranes the two septins behave similarly.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of fly and yeast septin behavior.

claim: Fly septins form similar structures on membranes containing PS or PI(4,5)P2, and the main determinant of fly septin binding and filament organization in both cases is the net surface charge of the membrane.
source: We find that fly septins form similar structures on membranes containing PS or PI(4,5)P2, and that the main determinant of fly septin binding and filament organization in both cases is the net surface charge of the membrane.
evidence: This is concluded from TIRF and EM experiments with different lipid compositions.

claim: Cdc11-capped yeast septin octamers are highly selective for PI, PI(4)P, PI(5)P and PI(4,5)P2, while they do not interact with PS.
source: By contrast, Cdc11-capped yeast septin octamers were shown to be highly selective for PI, PI(4)P, PI(5)P and PI(4,5)P2, while they did not interact with PS (Khan et al., 2018; Bridges et al., 2016; Bertin et al., 2010; Beber, 2018; Cannon et al., 2019; Bridges et al., 2014; Casamayor and Snyder, 2003; Onishi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on yeast septins.

claim: Septins interact with negatively charged phospholipids via a polybasic region close to the N-terminus that is composed of a sequence of 1–7 basic amino acids.
source: It is thought that septins interact with negatively charged phospholipids via a polybasic region close to the N-terminus that is composed of a sequence of 1–7 basic amino acids (Zhang et al., 1999; Casamayor and Snyder, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The polybasic stretch in septins is very similar to polybasic sequences found in gelsolin, profilin, G-protein-coupled receptor kinases and ion channels, which are all reported to interact with PI(4,5)P2.
source: This stretch is very similar to polybasic sequences found in gelsolin, profilin, G-protein-coupled receptor kinases and ion channels (Zhang et al., 1999), which are all reported to interact with PI(4,5)P2.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The intricate, highly organized septin filament meshworks observed at the membrane of dividing budding yeast have not been documented to date in animal cells.
source: It is noteworthy that the intricate, highly organized septin filament meshworks observed at the membrane of dividing budding yeast (Bertin et al., 2012; Ong et al., 2014) have not been documented to date in animal cells.
evidence: This is based on a review of the literature.

claim: Cdc11 and Shs1 have C-termini that are 2–3 times longer than their animal counterparts.
source: Cdc11/Shs1 have C-termini that are 2–3 times longer than their animal counterparts (118 and 211 residues for Cdc11 and Shs1 vs 55 and 57 residues for SEPT2 and DSep1, respectively).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: Cdc11 and Shs1 termini are predicted to form coiled-coils twice as long as the ones of SEPT2/DSep1.
source: Cdc11 and Shs1 termini are predicted to form coiled-coils twice as long as the ones of SEPT2/DSep1, and with flexible hinges between the α6 helix and the coiled-coils 2–3 times longer than their animal counterparts (Figure 1B,C and Taveneau et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on coiled-coil prediction analysis.

claim: The very high conservation between fly and mammalian septins (on the order of 65–75% identity) suggests that studying animal septin assembly promises to advance our understanding of how differences between yeast and animal septins lead to differences in their organization and function.
source: Given the above differences between yeast and animal septins, the very high conservation between fly and mammalian septins (on the order of 65–75% identity), and the ubiquitous presence and essential functions of animal septins, studying animal septin assembly promises to advance our understanding of how differences between yeast and animal septins lead to differences in their organization and function.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the research based on sequence conservation.
